title: The steadfast and the sharers
hookLine: the steadfast, those who meditated, shared food, ran the kitchen and wielded the sword

lines: THE MAN WHO SWEEPS THE STEPS.
cards: In a gurdwara kitchen somewhere, a woman has been on her feet since five in the morning, rolling more rotis than anyone could count. Nobody knows her full name; the kids just call her auntie ji.
She'll never be in a history book. Out front, a man has swept the same gurdwara steps every Sunday for thirty years.
The Ardas, having remembered the five, the four and the forty, now remembers people like them: not by name, but by what they did with their hands and their days. It's a list of verbs.

teach.b: Listen to the run of it: hathiaan, japiaan, tapiaan. The hathi are the steadfast, who held firm and wouldn't be moved off their faith. The japi kept the Name and the banis going, day after day.
The tapi lived with discipline and endured hardship. Then, what they did: jinhaan naam japiaa, who meditated on the Name.
Vand chhakiaa, who shared what they had, and then ate. Deg chalaaee, who kept the cooking pot going, who ran the langar. Tegh vaahee, who wielded the sword to protect others.

Vand chhakiaa is one of what Sikhs often call the three pillars: naam japna, remembering the Name; kirat karni, honest work; and vand chhakna, sharing. Sikh teachers like to point to the order: vand, then chhak.
Share, then eat, not eat and share the leftovers.

teach.h: THE POT AND THE SWORD, SIDE BY SIDE.
teach.b: The kitchen and the sword sit side by side, too. Deg and tegh: feeding and protecting, named together as two halves of looking after people. Those two words come back later in the Ardas.
Then the line names what these people left behind: their kamaaee, a word for earnings, what you earn by labor.
The Ardas asks the room to fix its mind on the kamaaee of these beloved, truthful ones. Not their fame. Their earnings, built up quietly, meal by meal and morning by morning.
So every time Sikhs pray, people like auntie ji are remembered, even if nobody there knows her name.

how: In every Ardas Sikhs remember the steadfast, those who meditated, shared their food, ran the langar and wielded the sword; vand chhakna, sharing, is counted among the three pillars of Sikh life.

o: a well-known deed that wins a person renown
earnings, what someone builds up by labor
a prayer recited before the langar meal

games.q: the steadfast and the sharers — tap the pairs.

s: vand chhakna means eat first, then share the leftovers
vand comes first: share, then eat.
the Ardas names the kitchen and the sword side by side
deg chalaaee, tegh vaahee: feeding and protecting together.
this part of the Ardas names each person it remembers
it remembers them by what they did, not by name.

games.q: you've made dinner and there's a neighbor who lives alone. by vand chhakna, what's the order?
games.why: vand chhakiaa: share first, then eat. it's one of the three pillars of Sikh life.

practice: Think through today's meals and pick one you could share: a little extra for a neighbor, an extra place at the table, or simply serving someone else first.
Picture yourself doing it, share first, then eat, and notice how small the act is, and how old. If you pray, say Waheguru as you decide.

wordCard.voice: Kamaaee, earnings built up quietly, meal by meal and morning by morning. Hathi, japi, tapi; those who shared, then ate, kept the pot going and held the sword: remembered for their kamaaee.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: vand chhakiaa, shared and then ate; the Ardas remembers those who did.

carryVoice: Your line: the sharers. First the sharing, then the meal, and nobody needs to know. Until tomorrow.
